## GPT: use language modeling to learn reusable weights {#gpt-pretraining .gpt-slide}

<p class="gpt-lead">The autoregressive objective is familiar. Its role here is to <strong>prepare a model for reuse</strong>.</p>

```{=html}
<svg class="gpt-corpus-flow" viewBox="0 0 1320 450" role="img" aria-label="Unlabeled corpus passages are tokenized into training windows. Familiar causal language modeling updates embeddings, decoder blocks, and vocabulary head. Save these learned weights as a pretrained checkpoint that can be reused for continuation or later task adaptation.">
<defs><marker id="gp-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10Z" fill="#0f7881"/></marker></defs>
<g font-family="sans-serif" fill="#17364a">
<rect x="15" y="45" width="330" height="245" rx="12" fill="#e8e6dc"/><text x="40" y="90" font-size="27" font-weight="bold">CORPUS PASSAGES</text><text x="40" y="145" font-size="28">“the cat sat on the mat”</text><text x="40" y="192" font-size="28">“the train arrived late”</text><text x="40" y="239" font-size="28">“the film was moving”</text>
<path d="M350 170H460" stroke="#0f7881" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#gp-arrow)"/>
<rect x="475" y="45" width="365" height="245" rx="12" fill="#dfece6"/><text x="657" y="91" font-size="27" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">CAUSAL LM TRAINING</text><text x="657" y="144" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">next-token loss</text><text x="657" y="194" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">gradients + updates</text><text x="657" y="244" font-size="25" text-anchor="middle">many text windows, batches</text>

<rect x="970" y="45" width="335" height="245" rx="12" fill="#17364a"/><text x="1137" y="91" font-size="27" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-weight="bold">SAVE CHECKPOINT θ*</text><text x="1137" y="147" font-size="27" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">embeddings</text><text x="1137" y="194" font-size="27" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">decoder blocks</text><text x="1137" y="241" font-size="27" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">vocabulary head</text>
<text x="180" y="340" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle">No task labels required</text><text x="657" y="340" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle">All model parameters learn</text><path d="M1137 300V365H660" stroke="#0f7881" stroke-width="3" fill="none" marker-end="url(#gp-arrow)"/><text x="880" y="420" font-size="28" text-anchor="middle">Reuse for continuation or later task adaptation</text>
</g></svg>
```

<p class="gpt-takeaway">Transfer the <strong>learned parameters</strong>, together with the model’s tokenizer and configuration.</p>
<p class="gpt-caption">The corpus supplies the supervision. Corpus selection and preprocessing shape what the model can learn.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Original teaching diagram. Berkeley CS288, PDF pp. 57–59; <a href="https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf">Radford et al. (2018), §3</a>. Authored corpus excerpts; no training run is shown.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. The instructor explicitly confirmed that prediction, causal
attention, and AR generation have already been taught. Do not rederive them.
The new point is the role of the learning stage: train on general text, then reuse
its weights rather than initialize every downstream model from scratch.

Trace the three passages into training windows. These are authored illustrations,
not a sample of a measured training corpus. Actual windows can contain multiple
sentences and are bounded by the model's context length; segmentation, document
boundaries, tokenization, filtering, and deduplication are data decisions. We will
study data and scale in Session 2. Corpus size alone does not define pretraining.

The familiar loss updates the token/position embeddings, decoder stack, and
vocabulary prediction mapping; tied parameters are shared rather than separately
counted. Save learned weights and keep their matching tokenizer/configuration.
A checkpoint is not a list of contextual vectors for these three sentences, nor
an explicit database of answers. Learned parameters can nevertheless memorize
training text. Do not imply that saving weights prevents memorization.

The original 2018 GPT work explicitly followed LM pretraining with supervised
adaptation. Thus decoder pretraining is relevant to understanding tasks as well
as continuation. Pretraining describes a stage in a reuse workflow; autoregressive
describes a prediction structure. Transition: “With the same text, how does this
recipe's supervision differ from BERT's?”
:::

## Same corpus. A different distribution of supervision. {#gpt-supervision .gpt-slide}

<p class="gpt-source"><span>ONE SOURCE WINDOW</span>the cat sat on the mat</p>
<div class="gpt-comparison">
<div><h3>BERT · selected recovery</h3><span class="lab-label">SUPPLIED INPUT</span><p class="gpt-example">the <b>[MASK]</b> sat on the <b>[MASK]</b></p><span class="lab-label">DIRECT LOSS TARGETS</span><p class="gpt-targets">cat · mat</p><p>Each selected prediction can use both sides of the corrupted input.</p></div>
<div><h3>GPT · causal language modeling</h3><span class="lab-label">SUPPLIED INPUT</span><p class="gpt-example">the cat sat on the</p><span class="lab-label">ALIGNED LOSS TARGETS</span><p class="gpt-targets">cat · sat · on · the · mat</p><p>Each prediction uses its observed prefix. Score each eligible next-token target.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="gpt-objective">

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{t=2}^{6}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})$$

</div>
<p class="gpt-caption">Familiar loss, shown for this window. Same corpus does not mean the same learning signal—or a guaranteed winner.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Example-based adaptation of Berkeley’s matched MLM/causal diagrams, PDF pp. 36 and 58; Stanford CS224N, PDF p. 31. Two BERT targets are illustrative, not a 15% sample. Boundary tokens omitted; the first word is supplied as context.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 4 minutes. Keep the purpose on pretraining supervision. Read the targets,
not another token-by-token generation trace. BERT's MLM part has selected loss
positions; GPT scores each eligible next-token target in its training window.
Here there is no start token: the first word is context, so there are five scored
targets. The final source token mat is the last label and needs no extra input
position for this example. Boundary/padding conventions affect actual counts.

The displayed GPT input is processed with the already familiar causal mask.
Although the complete prefix row is available to the training computation, a
prediction cannot access later input positions. Do not reopen the attention
matrix or the parallelism derivation. The equation is the known cross-entropy
objective averaged over five targets; x2 is cat and x6 is mat. There is no new
arithmetic task, and no new probability factorization to derive.

BERT's unselected context states can still receive gradients; no direct loss
at a position does not mean its representation is frozen. Selected-but-unchanged
and randomly replaced positions also contribute to BERT's MLM loss, even though
this illustration uses MASK for both. NSP is omitted to isolate the token-level
comparison, not silently removed from the historical BERT recipe.

More scored positions does not establish better representations. The available
context and task difficulty also differ; fair comparisons need controlled data,
model size, compute, and downstream evaluation. This slide reports no benchmark.
Transition: “After the optimization stage, what does the saved base model give us?”
:::

## A pretrained checkpoint is the result of learning {#gpt-base-model .gpt-slide .s1-slide}

<p class="gpt-lead">Follow the <strong>weights</strong> across the boundary between pretraining and use.</p>
<div class="lab-toolbar gpt-mode-buttons" role="group" aria-label="Inspect the weight lifecycle"><button type="button" data-gpt-mode="train" aria-pressed="true">Pretrain on text</button><button type="button" data-gpt-mode="use" aria-pressed="false">Use saved checkpoint</button></div>
<div class="gpt-lifecycle" aria-live="polite"><div><span class="lab-label">TEXT</span><p id="gpt-stage-text">Corpus window: the cat sat on the mat</p><span class="lab-label">SUPERVISION / OUTPUT</span><p id="gpt-stage-target">Observed next tokens supply the training targets.</p></div><div class="gpt-weight-panel"><span class="lab-label">PARAMETERS</span><strong id="gpt-weight-status">Weights change</strong><p id="gpt-stage-operation">Loss → gradients → optimizer update</p><p id="gpt-stage-result">Save the trained checkpoint for reuse.</p></div></div>
<p class="gpt-takeaway">A base model learns text continuation. Pretraining alone does not establish reliable instruction following.</p>
<p class="gpt-caption">Later task adaptation can update these weights again. Ordinary decoding does not.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Reuses the preserved training/generation example, narrowed to the weight lifecycle. The continuation is authored, not a measured prediction. Stanford CS224N, PDF p. 31; Berkeley CS288, PDF pp. 57–59. Adaptation and prompting are developed in Session 2.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Use the control once in each mode. This adapts the old deck's
#training-generation example: corpus prefix the cat → observed sat versus an
illustrative emitted continuation the cat sleeps. The earlier presentation's
comparison was static; this lightweight switch makes the weight status explicit.
It executes no model, training, random sampling, or optimizer. Do not turn it into
a second generation tutorial: the only teaching question is “Are weights changing?”

During pretraining, corpus targets enter the loss, and the optimizer updates the
parameters. At ordinary use, the saved model produces continuation probabilities
with fixed weights. A different input changes the activations and outputs, not
the stored weights. The displayed sleeps continuation is illustrative; it does
not claim a particular checkpoint would produce it. No ground-truth answer is
supplied to a loss in this ordinary decoding example.

A base model is the product of the pretraining stage, before whatever later task
adaptation or post-training we may choose. It can sometimes respond to instructions,
but the pretraining objective by itself does not ensure that it reliably behaves
as a helpful assistant. Do not assert an absolute inability. Likewise, the original
GPT transfer story involved supervised task adaptation, not just prompting.
Leave prompting examples, fine-tuning mechanics, and instruction tuning to their
agreed later sections. Transition: “Both recipes reuse text supervision. Must the
supplied text and the generated text occupy the same sequence?”
:::

<p class="gpt-question">How can we read the whole corrupted source while generating only what is missing?</p>
<p class="s1-source">Conceptual bridge to T5, not its exact sentinel-token format. Gap labels and outputs are authored targets. Stanford CS224N, PDF p. 36; Berkeley CS288, PDF p. 66.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 2 minutes. Synthesize the pretraining idea: an existing AR objective can
learn weights from corpus text, and those weights become reusable. We compared
the supervision rather than relearning the prediction machinery.

Return to the fixed cat sentence. All uncorrupted source words should remain
available to the reader, including words after a gap. The desired output is a
separate sequence of missing pieces. Point to the two streams: source and output.
The animated paths show information flow, not actual attention values or inference.
Gap A/B are explanatory placeholders, not T5's real sentinel strings. The output
labels are a conceptual request, not the exact training target serialization.

The unresolved box deliberately withholds T5's encoder–decoder training recipe.
Do not claim a decoder-only model could never implement conditional reconstruction;
we are motivating a useful alternative, not proving an exclusive capability.
No T5 equations, sentinel construction, or detailed architecture are taught here.
End with the displayed question and stop for instructor review.
:::
